# Fugaro CLI reference

Every command and flag `fugaro` ships, generated from the command tree
(`internal/cli.NewRootCmd`) by `go run ./ee/clidoc`. Cobra's own `help`
and `completion` commands, the root's `-v, --version` flag, and the
`-h, --help` flag of every command, are part of what `fugaro --help` lists,
so they are here too. Commands the CLI
hides are not listed: they are internal, and a hidden command is not user
documentation.

## `fugaro accounts clear`

Clear one account's broken or exhausted credential mark, after replacing its token

Clear one Claude account's credential mark, so the cascade may route work to it
again. This is an operator's command: it writes the project's own database,
acting as you (ADC), and it is the only thing that ends a broken mark.

Only the two states an operator's action is what ends may be cleared:

  broken     the service saw a 401 (D139) and nothing clears it on its own.
             Replace the token first, then clear the mark here.
  exhausted  the account reported a usage limit and holds until its reset time.

A backed-off mark is refused: a probe is what clears it (C1.12), and clearing it
by hand would route real work to a credential that has not answered since it was
held. A state this Fugaro does not know is refused too, because clearing it
could take off a hold a newer release placed.

The write is one node — creds/marks/NAME, in this installation's own database —
and it is conditional on the value read (PutIfMatch), so a mark the service
changed at the same moment is not lost: the write re-reads the mark and clears
it only while its state is still the one the confirmation named, so a 401 the
service recorded while you were reading is left for its own decision rather
than taken off with the hold you confirmed.

NAME is "default" (the repository's own unnamed claude-oauth-token secret), a
claude_accounts name of the selected project config, or an account the database
already carries a mark for — a mark is the account existing, and a name with
none of the three is refused rather than written, so a typo cannot leave a mark
node for a credential that does not exist. (A mark whose name this checkout's
claude_accounts does not list is the ordinary case for a project several
checkouts share: claude_accounts is per-checkout and never published, while the
marks are the project's own. fugaro doctor names such marks, so its fix has
to work here.) Nothing reads or prints a token value, a secret ID or a prefix
of one: names and states only.

This command is run by a person in the sense that it acts as you, with your own
credentials, on your own installation's database — but it is not one of the
commands that refuse a coding agent's session. It records no owner decision and
approves nothing: it takes off a hold the service placed, on a credential you
have already replaced the token for, and the service marks it broken again if
the token is still refused. fugaro budget set and fugaro budget kill — the
same kind of write to the same database, with the same credentials — refuse no
agent either, and fugaro allow-delete and fugaro managed flag, which do, are
commands whose own output is an approval of a later cloud change.

Usage: `fugaro accounts clear NAME`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--config` | string | "" | no | the project config file to use (default: the project's $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/fugaro/projects/<name>.yaml) |
| `--gcp-project` | string | "" | no | the GCP project ID; it must be the selected project config's gcp_project |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for clear |
| `--project` | string | "" | no | the Fugaro project to act on (default: the checkout's fugaro.yaml project:, else $FUGARO_PROJECT, else the only project config) |
| `--region` | string | "" | no | GCP region (overrides the project config's) |
| `--yes` | bool | `false` | no | skip the typed confirmation (read what it does first) |

This command has no subcommands.

## `fugaro accounts ls`

List the named Claude accounts (claude_accounts in the local config) a repository may use with fugaro run --token

List the names fugaro run --token NAME (and a repository's own agent.oauth_token)
accept for a repository: "default" (the repository's own unnamed
claude-oauth-token secret, always allowed) first, then every claude_accounts
name in the local config whose allow_data_to lists the repository, sorted
(config.AllowedClaudeAccounts, the one place that decides the question).

The names are a local, read-only lookup, offline whenever a project config is
already selected on this machine: it reads the local config file the CLI would
otherwise select for a cloud command, and never calls Secret Manager, never
reads or prints a token value, only names.

The state column is not local. When the selected project has a Firebase budget
backend (budget.rtdb_url, which fugaro update --firebase-project <gcp-project-id> writes), each account's
credential state is read from that database as you, with your Application
Default Credentials — the creds/marks subtree the credentials service writes,
which an admin's rules grant the read of — and printed beside the name as
available, exhausted until T, backed off or broken. A project with no backend,
and a machine where no project config could be selected, answer with the names
alone and a note saying why: the command never turns "could not read" into
"every account is available".

That read is bounded: five seconds for the whole of it (the token source, the
project check and the marks), one attempt per call, and no retry. A database
that is unreachable rather than refusing — a laptop offline, a firewall that
drops — therefore costs this command seconds, not the per-call timeout twice,
and the names are printed with a note saying the states could not be read.

--json's "complete" is false when no project config could be selected for a
reason other than an explicit --config/--project/$FUGARO_CONFIG/$FUGARO_PROJECT
(several project configs with nothing to pick one, for example): "accounts"
is then "default" alone, which may be short the repository's real
claude_accounts, not a true answer that none are configured; "note" says why.

Usage: `fugaro accounts ls`

Flags:

| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--config` | string | "" | no | the project config file to use (default: the project's $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/fugaro/projects/<name>.yaml) |
| `--gcp-project` | string | "" | no | the GCP project ID; it must be the selected project config's gcp_project |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for ls |
| `--json` | bool | `false` | no | print machine-readable output |
| `--project` | string | "" | no | the Fugaro project to act on (default: the checkout's fugaro.yaml project:, else $FUGARO_PROJECT, else the only project config) |
| `--region` | string | "" | no | GCP region (overrides the project config's) |
| `--repo` | string | "" | no | repository as owner/name (default: this checkout's origin) |

## `fugaro allow-delete`

Record the objects a run may delete or replace, by address (the project's owner)

Record which Terraform addresses the project's owner approves for deletion or
replacement, and which object at each address is approved, in a managed
project's fugaro/allow-delete.json at the root of the runs bucket. An approval
lives in that object and nowhere else: this command is Fugaro's only writer of
it, with the operator's own credentials.

An argument is an address and the identity of the object approved there,
written as ADDRESS=IDENTITY: the Terraform address a plan reports, as in
google_cloud_run_v2_job.web or module.web.google_storage_bucket.data,
followed by the identity a refused managed apply printed for the object that
address removes, as in

  fugaro allow-delete 'module.web.google_storage_bucket.data=type=google_storage_bucket project=proj-1234 name=data id=data-bucket instance=2026-01-02T03:04:05.678Z'

An approval is of one object and not of the address: the same address carrying
another object later — another name, a renamed or replaced resource, one moved
in from elsewhere — is not approved by it, so an entry an earlier apply already
used admits nothing more. The identity is compared character for character with
the one the plan's before view shows, so copy it from the refusal rather than
retyping it. A refusal prints it inside a sentence of its own, so copy the
identity up to and not including the ')' that closes that sentence's
parenthetical — pasting that bracket as well is forgiven, once, since the
sentence put it there; one matched pair of double quotes is stripped the same
way, because a shell or a message may have added them (a quote at one end only
is a character of the identity, and is kept). What is not forgiven is any other
parenthesis: an identity holds none — a value's '(' and ')' are escaped with
everything else this program's printers would touch — so an argument that still
holds one is refused rather than recorded as an entry that would match no
removal. The two ends agree byte for byte because the identity is written in an
escaped form — a space in a value as \x20, a backslash as \\, a parenthesis as
\x28 and \x29, any other byte with no printable form as \xHH, and every byte a
shell reads in a way of its own — a separator, a pipe, a redirection, a
substitution, a quote, a glob, an expansion — as \xHH as well, so that what a
refusal prints holds no byte that can begin, end or continue a command, and is
exactly what a plan shows. Two bytes a shell rewrites are in it all the same,
because the form needs them: the single space between two parts, and the
backslash that introduces an escape. A paste that does not keep those two whole
arrives here as several arguments and is refused rather than recorded — nothing
is written, and no entry is made that would match no removal — but the identity
has to reach this command as one argument, byte for byte as the plan shows it,
for the loop to close. An identity longer than 8192
characters is refused here and by the plan: no refusal prints one, and the plan
refuses the removal rather than matching a printed part of it, so recording it
would be an approval that deletes nothing.

What the identity tells apart, and what it does not, said here rather than left
to be discovered. For the seven managed types whose state carries a value the
provider mints once per instance — a bucket's time_created, a secret's or an
artifact repository's create_time, a Cloud Run job's or an API key's uid, a
service account's unique_id, a bucket object's generation — the identity
carries that value, so an object of one of those types deleted and then created
again under the same name at the same address carries a DIFFERENT identity and
this entry no longer approves its removal. It does not for the seven types that
have no such value: a Cloud Scheduler job, a project service, and the five
*_iam_member types, whose whole state is the grant they carry. For those the
identity is the named object, and a re-creation under the same name at the same
address is approved by the entry that named it. The provider's own id is not
one of the instance values: for every managed type it is derived from the
configured name (an API key's id is projects/P/locations/global/keys/NAME).
If the difference matters for a resource of the second kind, review the list
rather than rely on the entry having been used up.

Nothing else is recorded — no note and no reason: the object's own version
history is the record of who approved what and when, and the identity is what
the approved delete is identified by.

Run it in your own terminal, as an operator, with your own credentials. Pass
the entries to approve, and they replace the list: an invocation that leaves an
entry out removes that approval, so the command names the entries it would drop
and asks for the project's name before writing such a list. With no arguments
the command prints the list — each entry in the same ADDRESS=IDENTITY form —
and writes nothing; it never empties the list, because an empty list is what an
absent one already means. A printed line is one you can paste back as far as its
IDENTITY half goes: the command that recorded the entry escaped it, so the
printers leave it alone and a line inside the listing's own bound carries it
back byte for byte. The address half is the plan's own — not escaped here and
not bounded here — so an address holding a tab, a run of spaces or a byte
outside printable ASCII is printed as the printers rewrite it: that line is not
the entry, and pasting it back records an entry about an address no plan has,
which the plan refuses rather than deleting anything. A line longer than twice
the identity's own bound is printed through the bounded sanitiser instead, cut
and marked as cut: what you read there is visibly a text and not an entry. The
entry itself is unchanged in the object either way.

What the object is for: a run's own credentials cannot write it, and the
deployer account a managed apply impersonates will not be able to (D75, Task
1.5), so a managed apply can take its allow-list from the owner's object
instead of from the command line of whatever session is applying: fugaro
managed apply reads this object and takes no address flag of its own, so the
session that applies cannot widen the list. (the converge still honours its own
--allow-delete on its own command line, where the addresses go to tf.Guard
directly.) What this does not do: a coding agent's session holds the
operator's credentials, so it can write this object directly (gcloud storage
cp) or unset its agent marker and run this command itself. The refusal below is a speed bump against
an agent that uses the program, not a boundary against one that goes around it
(SECURITY.md records the wider Owner/Editor bypass).

On a project that is not managed, this writes an object nothing reads: the
check below is that the bucket is the project's own runs bucket, which every
installation has, not that the project is Fugaro-managed.

The list is read fail-closed: an absent object, an empty one, one naming
another project, one written by an older Fugaro (its addresses carry no
identities, so nothing in it says which object was approved), one whose
identities are an earlier build's (an entry that names the object without the
per-instance value its type has matches no removal the gate identifies, so it
approves nothing — re-approve it from a current refusal), one whose fields
are not exactly the ones this command writes, or one this package cannot read
is no entries — and no entries refuses every delete and replacement rather
than permitting them. The write is fail-closed too: if the current list cannot
be read, nothing is written, and the write is conditioned on the object being
unchanged since that read, so a concurrent write is never silently overwritten
(run the command again).

Usage: `fugaro allow-delete [ADDRESS=IDENTITY...]`

| `--config` | string | "" | no | the project config file to use (default: the project's $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/fugaro/projects/<name>.yaml) |
| `--gcp-project` | string | "" | no | the GCP project ID; it must be the selected project config's gcp_project |

## `fugaro artifacts`

List and download what an artifact run delivered

Read and fetch the files a `mode: artifact` run put in the runs bucket.

Both subcommands read the run's result.json, never a bucket listing: ls prints
the record's own table, and get is the object — so an artifact the record names
and the bucket no longer holds (they expire with the run, runs_days) is a
recorded row that ls shows and a `get` that says exactly that.

The record was written by an untrusted, model-driven run, so get treats every
name in it as hostile: it downloads into a fresh directory it creates
(./<run>-artifacts/, with --out naming that directory's parent), refuses a name
that is absolute, walks out of that directory or begins with a dot, refuses to
overwrite an existing file without --force, and verifies the recorded size and
sha256 as the bytes arrive, leaving nothing behind when they do not match.
What it writes is never opened, executed or unpacked.

Usage: `fugaro artifacts`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for artifacts |

Subcommands:

- `fugaro artifacts get` -- Download a run's artifacts, verifying them against its record
- `fugaro artifacts ls` -- List what a run's record says it delivered

## `fugaro artifacts get`

Download a run's artifacts, verifying them against its record

Download one artifact NAME, or every artifact the record lists when NAME is
omitted, verifying each one's size and sha256 against the run's result.json as
the bytes arrive. A mismatch is an error naming both hashes, and nothing is
written — not even the file the download streamed into.

The destination is a fresh directory this command creates,
./<run-id>-artifacts/ unless --out names another parent for it. A name in the
record that is absolute, walks out of that directory, begins with a dot or
holds a control character is refused — a refusal, never a flattened name.
An existing file needs --force to be replaced.

Nothing downloaded is ever opened, executed or unpacked: the recorded content
type, the size and the sha256 are printed, and that is all. The sha256 proves
the bytes are the bytes the run uploaded; it is not tamper evidence.

Usage: `fugaro artifacts get RUN [NAME]`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--config` | string | "" | no | the project config file to use (default: the project's $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/fugaro/projects/<name>.yaml) |
| `--force` | bool | `false` | no | replace a file that is already at a destination path |
| `--gcp-project` | string | "" | no | the GCP project ID; it must be the selected project config's gcp_project |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for get |
| `--out` | string | "" | no | the directory to create the run's artifact directory in (default: the working directory) |
| `--project` | string | "" | no | the Fugaro project to act on (default: the checkout's fugaro.yaml project:, else $FUGARO_PROJECT, else the only project config) |
| `--region` | string | "" | no | GCP region (overrides the project config's) |
| `--repo` | string | "" | no | the repository RUN belongs to (owner/name; needed only for a bare run ID) |

This command has no subcommands.

## `fugaro artifacts ls`

the probe's verdict. The record is shown as it is — a name `get` cannot
retrieve is listed with the reason, never filtered out, and a missing object is
not ls's to hide: ls is the record, get is the object.

--json prints the record's artifact list verbatim.

## `fugaro backends ls`

List the compute backends this fugaro knows and which one the project uses

List the compute backends a project config's backend: key may name, and
which one the selected project uses:

  cloud-run    Cloud Run jobs (the default, and the one every installation
               runs on today)
  cloud-batch  Cloud Batch jobs, one VM per run (the VM backend)

A config that names no backend runs on cloud-run. A config that names
cloud-batch is refused by this build ("not enabled yet"): the backend and its
opener are built and tested, and nothing selects them until Fugaro has passed
the live checklist for it.

This is a local, read-only lookup: it reads the project config and the backend
names internal/backend defines, and it calls no cloud API. With --json it
prints one object instead of two lines, carrying the list, the selected project
and the name its config selects.

## `fugaro backlog`

File a backlog item, read the backlog, regenerate its index

Read the backlog in docs/backlog/, file an item into it, and regenerate
its index.

The backlog is one Markdown file per item, named `<id>-<slug>.md`, beside
the generated index README.md and the hand-written format FORMAT.md. The
naming rule is what lets two pull requests file an item at once: they write
two differently named files, and the merge is a union of disjoint files
rather than a conflict (D26). `add` writes one item under that rule and
refuses the one the folder already holds — the same title filed twice on
the same day. The index is derived state — regenerated,
never merged by hand — so two branches that regenerated it at once are
reconciled by re-running `fugaro backlog index`, and never by merging the
file (D28). `add` regenerates it in the same commit that files the item;
`index` regenerates it alone; `list` writes nothing and prints what the
index would say.

Nothing here reaches a network, a credential or an installation: the items
and the index are files in this checkout.

Usage: `fugaro backlog`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for backlog |

Subcommands:

- `fugaro backlog add` -- File an item in docs/backlog/ and regenerate the index
- `fugaro backlog index` -- Regenerate docs/backlog/README.md from the item files beside it
- `fugaro backlog list` -- Print the backlog's items as the index lists them

## `fugaro backlog add`

File an item in docs/backlog/ and regenerate the index

File an item, and regenerate the index beside it.

The item takes the next id for the day it is filed (D26) and is written
as `<id>-<slug>.md`, with the eight front-matter fields the format
requires (D27). The index is regenerated in the same command, so the
commit that files an item is the commit that regenerates the index.

--title and --why are required, and so is --filed-by: an item is not a
title with no text, and who filed it is one of the eight fields. An item
is committed, so a --filed-by with an @ in it records `unknown`. --what
defaults to the title, and --done and --link are written when given.

An item filed by hand records `mode: none` — no run chose a mode for it.
--mode names the mode a run resolved when the item is about one, and
--filed-in says where it came from: `hand`, `run:<run id>` or
`pr:<number>`.

Usage: `fugaro backlog add`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--area` | string | `repo` | no | the area the item is about: an area name, project or repo |

## `fugaro backlog index`

Regenerate docs/backlog/README.md from the item files beside it

Regenerate the backlog's index from the item files.

The index lists one row per item — the id linked to its file, the title,
the mode, the area, the status, who filed it and the date — sorted by id,
with the closed and dropped rows grouped under the open ones, under a
count line (D28). It is written to <dir>/README.md, and it is the only
file this command touches.

The document is a pure function of the item files: every date in it comes
from the item that carries it and no clock is read, so regenerating an
unchanged folder rewrites the same bytes and a regeneration in review
diffs only where an item changed (D27). A pull request that adds an item
runs this in the same commit, and a test in internal/cli fails on an index
that is not current — which is why the file is never merged by hand.

Usage: `fugaro backlog index`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--dir` | string | `docs/backlog` | no | the folder the item files live in |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for index |

Subcommands:

This command has no subcommands.

## `fugaro backlog list`

Print the backlog's items as the index lists them

Print the backlog's items.

The output is the index itself, rendered from the item files rather than
read back from README.md: a stale index on disk cannot change what this
prints, and a reader who sees a difference between the two has found the
file that needs `fugaro backlog index`.

--json prints one document instead: {dir, items[{id, title, mode, area,
status, filed_by, filed_in, date, path}], open, closed, dropped}, indented.
The rows are the index's own rows in the index's own order, and the three
counts are the count line's own figures, so a screen shows what the
Markdown says rather than a second reading of the folder.

Nothing is written, and nothing is reached over the network: a folder that
does not exist is an error rather than an empty backlog.

Usage: `fugaro backlog list`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--dir` | string | `docs/backlog` | no | the folder the item files live in |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for list |
| `--json` | bool | `false` | no | print machine-readable output |

Look at and change the project's budget: the caps, today's counters, the kill

Database (design §8). show needs the Viewer role on the Firebase project;

editors, and terraform.budget_admins). preview needs the Viewer role too,

## `fugaro budget kill`

Halt every run of the project or of one repository (budget admins)

Set the project's kill switch (--all) or one repository's (--repo [owner/name]),
recording who, when and why. --repo with no value means the repository this
checkout belongs to, as it does for set. show takes owner/name (its empty
--repo means no repository filter, not a checkout), and preview already
means this checkout's repository without the flag.
Runs in flight halt within seconds (a run in its last stage finishes pushing
its work first) and new runs refuse. --all asks you to type the project's name
(or pass --yes); one repository needs no confirmation.

Usage: `fugaro budget kill (--all | --repo [owner/name]) [--reason TEXT]`

| `--gcp-project` | string | "" | no | the GCP project ID; it must be the selected project config's gcp_project |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for kill |
| `--project` | string | "" | no | the Fugaro project to act on (default: the checkout's fugaro.yaml project:, else $FUGARO_PROJECT, else the only project config) |
| `--reason` | string | "" | no | why (recorded, shown by budget show and watch) |
| `--region` | string | "" | no | GCP region (overrides the project config's) |
| `--repo` | string | "" | no | one repository, given as owner/name (no value: this checkout's origin) |
| `--yes` | bool | `false` | no | confirm without typing the project's name |

## `fugaro budget preview`

Estimate a batch's worst-case model spend against today's caps

Estimate what N runs of a recipe may cost at most, and how that compares
with today's remaining daily caps. It is a ceiling, not a forecast: a run
is bounded by the smaller of budget.per_run_usd and the recipe's most
stages times the repository's agent.max_budget_usd.

That figure is the model ceiling and nothing else: a run also bills for
the machine it asked for, and no budget key bounds compute at all --
the run's own timeout is the cap.
So for every workflow the checkout defines the preview also prints a
compute ceiling -- the workflow's own resources over its own
timeouts.total, at this installation's compute prices -- and says out
loud that it is NOT CAPPED, because for a run whose expensive half is a
render on a big machine the model ceiling is not the worst case. The
basis is timeouts.total and not a render step's own timeout: a render
that overruns still burns the run's clock to the deadline. Without a
price table for the installation's region the line names what is
missing and prints no dollar figure, rather than $0.00.

When the repository's recorded runs of the last 30 days are at least 5,
the preview also prints, clearly labelled typical:, what one run of the
recipe usually costs: the mean recorded cost of each stage kind (on the
model the checkout pins for it, with the recipe's role mapping applied as
a run applies it), at the recipe's typical stage count -- one round of
each loop the recipe and its round knobs leave in, the two fix stages
sharing one mean -- over the runs of the window, whatever they ended as:
a stage counts once it recorded a cost. A kind the window has no cost
for on that model leaves the line out and names the model, rather than
pricing the pinned model with what another one cost. Runs the figure
cannot use are said to be left out, never counted as runs that cost
nothing: a run whose model_usd was a subscription's rather than a bill
(agent.auth oauth, or a cascade run the plan served in full), a
result.json that is missing or unreadable, and a record with no
per-stage cost at all (one from before the runner kept it, or
stages that all cost nothing).

The recipe resolves as it does for a run: the repository's
.fugaro/recipes, the project's published recipes, then the catalog. The
knobs come from the checkout's fugaro.yaml; without a checkout of the
repository here, agent.max_budget_usd is unknown and only
budget.per_run_usd bounds the figure, so with neither the preview says it
is unbounded.

It reads the database's caps and today's counters (the Viewer role), and
the repository's runs (the runs bucket, for the typical line). A recipe
that is not in the checkout also reads the project's recipes from the
runs bucket, as recipes ls does, which a plain project Viewer cannot
read (the converge removes that access): not reading it costs the project layer,
and the ceiling with it. The typical line's own read of the bucket is
the one that costs the line and nothing else: a bucket it cannot read
leaves the ceiling standing. It writes nothing.

Usage: `fugaro budget preview --recipe NAME --runs N [--repo R]`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--config` | string | "" | no | the project config file to use (default: the project's $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/fugaro/projects/<name>.yaml) |
| `--gcp-project` | string | "" | no | the GCP project ID; it must be the selected project config's gcp_project |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for preview |
| `--json` | bool | `false` | no | print machine-readable output |
| `--project` | string | "" | no | the Fugaro project to act on (default: the checkout's fugaro.yaml project:, else $FUGARO_PROJECT, else the only project config) |
| `--recipe` | string | "" | yes | the recipe to preview (default, lint-fix, pick, premium, review-only, run-digest, solo, standard, test-and-fix) |
| `--region` | string | "" | no | GCP region (overrides the project config's) |
| `--repo` | string | "" | no | the repository (owner/name); default: the checkout's origin |
| `--runs` | int | `0` | yes | how many runs to estimate |

This command has no subcommands.

## `fugaro budget set`

Set a cap, the lease limit or the mode (budget admins)

Set caps in the project's budget database, with an ETag-guarded write that shows
the old and the new value.

  --global            the project's daily and per-run caps; also takes --max-reserve and --mode
  --defaults          the caps of every repository that has none of its own
  --repo [owner/name] one repository's caps; --repo with no value means the
                      repository this checkout belongs to, which needs no
                      owner/name at all

--max-reserve (the largest single lease) and --mode (observe, or enforce: caps
bite) are project-wide, so they go with --global. Amounts are US dollars from 0
to 100000, and a per-run cap may not exceed the daily cap of the same scope.
--clear removes the scope's caps.

--repo owner/name always works, from anywhere; the bare --repo is refused
outside a checkout whose origin names a repository, and never stands for the
project-wide caps. kill and resume take --repo the same way. preview needs no
bare form: left out, --repo already means this checkout's repository. show is
the one whose empty --repo is not the checkout (it means no repository
filter), so it takes owner/name.

Raising a cap (setting one that was unset counts), or lowering the mode to
observe, loosens what runs may spend, so it asks you to type the project's name
(or pass --yes). Lowering needs no confirmation.

Usage: `fugaro budget set (--global | --defaults | --repo [owner/name]) [--daily USD] [--per-run USD] [--max-reserve USD] [--mode observe|enforce] | --clear`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--clear` | bool | `false` | no | remove the scope's caps |
| `--config` | string | "" | no | the project config file to use (default: the project's $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/fugaro/projects/<name>.yaml) |
| `--daily` | float64 | `0` | no | the daily cap, in US dollars |
| `--defaults` | bool | `false` | no | the default caps of repositories without their own |
| `--gcp-project` | string | "" | no | the GCP project ID; it must be the selected project config's gcp_project |
| `--global` | bool | `false` | no | the project's own caps |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for set |
| `--max-reserve` | float64 | `0` | no | the largest single lease, in US dollars (with --global) |
| `--mode` | string | "" | no | observe or enforce (with --global) |
| `--per-run` | float64 | `0` | no | the per-run cap, in US dollars |
| `--project` | string | "" | no | the Fugaro project to act on (default: the checkout's fugaro.yaml project:, else $FUGARO_PROJECT, else the only project config) |
| `--region` | string | "" | no | GCP region (overrides the project config's) |
| `--repo` | string | "" | no | one repository's caps, given as owner/name (no value: this checkout's origin) |
| `--yes` | bool | `false` | no | confirm a raise without typing the project's name |

## `fugaro budget show`

Show caps, today's counters, kill switches, headroom and the runs in flight

Show the project's budget: the mode, the caps, today's (UTC) counted, spent and
notional dollars, the headroom under the caps, the kill switches and the runs
in flight. By default the global figures and the project config's
repositories; --repo one repository; --all every repository the database
knows. Notional is a subscription's list-price figure, never billed and never
capped. Counted is spent plus what runs have reserved and not released; --json
carries that difference as leased_usd, the money leased and not yet spent: a
crashed run's lease is never released, so it stays in the figure for the rest
of the day. --compute adds each repository's compute dollars, read from the
runs bucket: a run's compute is in its own record and nowhere in the
database, so the flag costs a listing of the bucket's repositories and, for
each repository shown, a listing of its runs minted since the previous day
began plus a read of every one of those records (a run's start day is only
known once its record is read), and everything that only needs the counters
leaves it off. The figure is an estimate by design, priced from each run's
own price table, and covers the runs that started today and recorded a
result: a run still in flight has recorded none, so today's is partial, and
a repository whose runs recorded no estimate is null, never 0.

Usage: `fugaro budget show`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--all` | bool | `false` | no | every repository in the database |
| `--compute` | bool | `false` | no | also read each repository's compute dollars from the runs bucket (an estimate; null and n/a where the day's runs recorded none) |
| `--config` | string | "" | no | the project config file to use (default: the project's $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/fugaro/projects/<name>.yaml) |
| `--gcp-project` | string | "" | no | the GCP project ID; it must be the selected project config's gcp_project |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for show |
| `--json` | bool | `false` | no | print machine-readable output |
| `--project` | string | "" | no | the Fugaro project to act on (default: the checkout's fugaro.yaml project:, else $FUGARO_PROJECT, else the only project config) |
| `--region` | string | "" | no | GCP region (overrides the project config's) |
| `--repo` | string | "" | no | only this repository (owner/name) |

This command has no subcommands.

## `fugaro cancel`

Cancel a run, letting the runner open a draft PR first

Cancel RUN (<repo-slug>/<run-id>, or a bare run ID).

cancel writes the run's cancel marker; the runner sees it, stops the current
stage and finalizes a draft PR. If the execution is still in a stage after
--grace, cancel stops it through Cloud Run. It never stops a run that is
opening its PR (finalize) or writing back its cache: it waits up to 10 more
minutes for finalize, and counts writeback as finalized. --grace is never
shorter than the workflow's timeouts.finalize_reserve (5m when neither the run
nor this checkout tells) plus 40s for the runner to notice the cancel. --now
stops the execution at once (so it takes no --grace), without waiting for the
draft PR, but still not mid-finalize.

Usage: `fugaro cancel RUN`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--config` | string | "" | no | the project config file to use (default: the project's $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/fugaro/projects/<name>.yaml) |
| `--gcp-project` | string | "" | no | the GCP project ID; it must be the selected project config's gcp_project |
| `--grace` | duration | `3m0s` | no | how long to wait for the runner to finalize before cancelling the execution (at least the run's finalize reserve plus 40s) |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for cancel |
| `--json` | bool | `false` | no | print the result as JSON |
| `--now` | bool | `false` | no | cancel the execution at once, without waiting for a draft PR |
| `--project` | string | "" | no | the Fugaro project to act on (default: the checkout's fugaro.yaml project:, else $FUGARO_PROJECT, else the only project config) |
| `--region` | string | "" | no | GCP region (overrides the project config's) |

## `fugaro completion bash`

Generate the autocompletion script for bash

Generate the autocompletion script for the bash shell.

This script depends on the 'bash-completion' package.
If it is not installed already, you can install it via your OS's package manager.

To load completions in your current shell session:

	source <(fugaro completion bash)

To load completions for every new session, execute once:

#### Linux:

	fugaro completion bash > /etc/bash_completion.d/fugaro

#### macOS:

	fugaro completion bash > $(brew --prefix)/etc/bash_completion.d/fugaro

You will need to start a new shell for this setup to take effect.

resolve a checkout too, but a read writes nothing, whoever runs it — the

with "valid": false and a reason, and is never silently dropped. The
paths are local state: they are never published to the runs bucket, to
the shared config or to any log.

works outside a checkout and with no config at all (an empty list).

## `fugaro coordinator`

The coordinator's deterministic half (docs/coordinator/implementation-plan.md).
Nothing here holds a model credential, a service of its own or a store of its
own: these commands read what fugaro already reads.

Advisory, never authoritative: a collision is reported and never blocks,
reorders or refuses a merge (spec §3).

Usage: `fugaro coordinator`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for coordinator |

- `fugaro coordinator report` -- Declare the work you are about to start
- `fugaro coordinator status` -- Show the work in flight, and where it collides

## `fugaro coordinator report`

Declare the work you are about to start

Write one intent record for this project's repository: the branch and the
target release the caller declares, and the files and services it is about
to touch, so that work still in flight can be seen before code exists
(spec §6).

The record's ID is derived from the caller and the declaration, and from
nothing else: reporting the same declaration twice writes ONE document, and
the second report replaces the first rather than adding to it.

The caller is who the local config names (user:), else git config
user.email, and a report nobody can be named for is refused: every record
is somebody's declaration, and one nobody can be named for is not one. That
name is a declaration too — nothing verifies it, and nothing authorises
anything by it (finding #11).

This command writes and reads nothing back: it prints the record it wrote
and issues no advice, which is the coordinator's whole posture in v1
(spec §3, advisory and never authoritative).

The write goes through the caller's own credentials, on the project's
budget.rtdb_url database. The rules grant /coordinator a read and no write
to anyone, so the write is admitted by the database role its caller holds
(roles/firebasedatabase.admin, which terraform.budget_admins have); a
launcher who is not an admin reports through the coordinator's front door
once it is deployed.

Usage: `fugaro coordinator report`

| `--file` | stringArray | `[]` | no | a path you are about to touch (repeatable) |

| `--release` | string | "" | no | the target release (default: the one the branch names, e.g. release/v0.11.0) |
| `--repo` | string | "" | no | the repository this report is about (owner/name; default: the local config's, when it lists one) |

## `fugaro coordinator status`

Show the work in flight, and where it collides

Join a repository's pull requests with its run records and print the view:
each pull request, the runs behind it, the branch and target release it declares,
the files and services those runs touched, and every pair of work still in
flight that touches the same file or service.

One repository by default, every repository the local config lists with --all,
which prints a view per repository and compares nothing across them: a service
is a path's shape in one tree, so two repositories' paths say nothing about
each other.

The pull requests listed are the ones the runs name, and that is the whole of
the list this reader can produce: gitprov reads one pull request by number and
has no call that lists a repository's (finding #10), so a pull request no run
names is never asked for. The rule the join is written to — a pull request no
run names is listed as having none, because it is work somebody has open and
dropping it is the one thing this view must not do — is not reached by this
command today.

Every repository is read through the coordinator's own credential: an
installation token for that repository, minted from the GitHub App the
environment holds and carrying a named read-only permission set — pull
requests and metadata, the two reads this view makes (Q3 answered (A)) —
and cached for the token's life, so a second read of the same repository
mints nothing. Every token the command minted is revoked when it is done,
so the credential lives for the read and no longer.
With FUGARO_CREDENTIALS_SERVICE_URL set, the installation's credentials
service holds the App's key and this command holds none, so it refuses (exit 1)
before it reads the App's ID or key: the service mints a run's token, and this
read is not a run.
Exit codes: 1 for a missing or malformed App credential (or the refusal above),
2 for a failure of the host.
The coordinator reads github only: a bitbucket repository is refused, and the
refusal names the reason, because its credential is one repository's access
token and cannot be widened to a project (reconciliation Q12 (A), finding #30).

--from-store is a different read of the same view (D364): it prints what the
sweep already stored, coordinator/repos/<slug>/ in the project's database,
through the caller's own credentials — roles/firebasedatabase.viewer is what
admits it — and with the same --repo and --all selection as above. It opens no
host and holds no App ID, no App key and no Bitbucket credential: everything a
stored view says about a pull request is what the sweep read once. It is the
read a console makes, and it works with FUGARO_CREDENTIALS_SERVICE_URL set,
where the read above refuses.
With --json, one repository is printed as it is stored: {"repo":
"owner/name", "stored": true, "view": {the view document}, "stale": {the
sweep's marker, as stored}}. A repository the coordinator has never
reconciled is "stored": false, and the document then holds the runs half of
the view — the runs bucket alone, with the pull requests those runs name
listed and no host state for them — so a console reads a project whose
coordinator is off with the same argv. --since bounds that half, and a
stored view is printed as the sweep wrote it. What decides between the two
is the database and never the local config: a teammate's config is the
published shared one, and it does not carry the coordinator's switch at all.
The stale marker is printed exactly as stored, with no age computed from it:
the stored view carries no time by design (internal/coordinator/sweep.go).

The launcher of a run is printed as what it is — the string the run's own launch
record wrote about itself — and never as an identity.

This command writes nothing of its own: no service, no model credential, and no
store it maintains. Without --from-store it reads nothing of the coordinator's
either — it is the read the CLI already performs, the runs bucket and a pull
request read that can only read — while --from-store reads the view the sweep
stored and nothing else.

Usage: `fugaro coordinator status`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--all` | bool | `false` | no | read every repository the local config lists, one view each |
| `--config` | string | "" | no | the project config file to use (default: the project's $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/fugaro/projects/<name>.yaml) |
| `--from-store` | bool | `false` | no | print the view the sweep stored, with no host read and no key (falls back to the runs alone when none is stored) |
| `--gcp-project` | string | "" | no | the GCP project ID; it must be the selected project config's gcp_project |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for status |
| `--json` | bool | `false` | no | print machine-readable output |
| `--project` | string | "" | no | the Fugaro project to act on (default: the checkout's fugaro.yaml project:, else $FUGARO_PROJECT, else the only project config) |
| `--region` | string | "" | no | GCP region (overrides the project config's) |
| `--repo` | string | "" | no | the repository to read (owner/name; default: the local config's, when it lists one) |
| `--since` | string | `7d` | no | only runs started within this long (7d, 36h, 90m; 0 for all) |

## `fugaro creds ls`

List the credentials the bundle secret holds: names and metadata, never a value (the owner)

List the credentials the credentials service's bundle secret holds: one row
per credential in the document, with its NAME, whether it is PRESENT, and the
document's last-changed time (the container's newest version metadata).

NAME is the name in the document's own spelling — the name fugaro creds set
takes. A named Claude account's row is claude-oauth-token-<account>, where <account>
is the account the policy's accounts block speaks.

Nothing else is printed: never a value, never a prefix of one, never a length
that would narrow a guess. --json carries the same shape.

The listing needs the container to exist, and it needs its newest version to be
one the service could read: an absent container, a container with no version, an
unreadable payload, a document the service's own loader refuses, and a version
that is DISABLED are each a named failure, never an empty list — a listing that
answered nothing for any of them would read as "the bundle holds no credential"
while the service is in fact issuing from one this command could not read.

It is refused from a coding agent's session and from a run's process, before
anything is read.

Usage: `fugaro creds ls`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |

| `--gcp-project` | string | "" | no | the GCP project ID; it must be the selected project config's gcp_project |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for ls |
| `--json` | bool | `false` | no | print machine-readable output |
| `--project` | string | "" | no | the Fugaro project to act on (default: the checkout's fugaro.yaml project:, else $FUGARO_PROJECT, else the only project config) |
| `--region` | string | "" | no | GCP region (overrides the project config's) |

## `fugaro creds set`

Set or replace one credential in the credentials service's bundle secret (the owner)

Set or replace one credential in the credentials service's bundle, the ONE
Secret Manager secret the service reads (Q6). The bundle is a YAML document
whose keys are credential names and whose values are the credentials; this
command reads it, sets or replaces the entry NAME and writes it back as a new
version, and then disables the version it replaced.

NAME is a credential the service can issue, in the document's own spelling:

  claude-oauth-token                    the default Claude account's OAuth token (tier A)
  claude-oauth-token-<account>       a named Claude account's OAuth token (tier A)
  anthropic-api-key                the project's Anthropic API key (tier B)
  github-app-key                  the GitHub App's private key (no tier: the mint signs with it)
  bitbucket-token                   the upstream Bitbucket token (no tier: held for the git proxy a later release adds; a Bitbucket run's job still uses its own mounted token)

The value is read only from stdin: pipe or redirect it in
(fugaro creds set claude-oauth-token < token-file), or, when stdin is a terminal, paste it
at a hidden prompt. It is never taken from an argument, a flag or the
environment, and never printed. One trailing newline (\n or \r\n) is dropped,
and the command says so. A value must be 4 bytes to 8192, on one line, with
no whitespace at either end; a longer value is a document the service's loader
would refuse, so it is refused here instead.

github-app-key is the ONE multi-line entry: it is an RSA private key in a PEM,
so it has to come in on stdin, from the key file the App's page downloads
(fugaro creds set github-app-key < PATH-TO-THE-KEY-FILE) — the hidden prompt reads one
line and cannot take a paste of a whole key, so it refuses this name and says
so. The value must be exactly one PEM block, its -----BEGIN line to its
matching -----END line and nothing else, and it must be a key the service's
mint can parse (internal/gitprov/github's ParsePrivateKey: PKCS#1 "RSA PRIVATE
KEY" or PKCS#8 "PRIVATE KEY", RSA). A single line of anything, a PEM with a
line of text around it, and a key the mint cannot use are each refused before
the write, and no refusal repeats a byte of the value.

The write is a read-modify-write of one document: the other entries keep their
bytes, and the whole document is parsed with the service's own loader
(internal/credsvc) before it is written, so what this command stores is what
the service accepts. After the write the bundle is read back and compared: if
it is not the document this command wrote, another write landed underneath and
this one lost it, which is said plainly and exits non-zero. Nothing is retried
silently.

A verified write then DISABLES the version it replaced, which the output names:
a rotated-away bundle that stays enabled keeps every superseded credential
readable by anyone who can read the container, which is the one thing a
rotation is for. Terraform cannot do this (it creates the container and manages
no version), so the command that writes a version retires the one before it. A
disable that fails is reported on stderr and does not fail the command: the new
credential is live either way.

The command needs the container to exist — the installation's Terraform creates
it (Task C1.18) and no command of ours does — and it works with the owner's own
project IAM (Project Owner or Editor: secretmanager.versions.get, .add and
.disable). There is no service account, no actAs and no operator grant on this
container: a secretVersionAdder on it is the ability to read every credential
in the bundle at once.

It is refused from a coding agent's session and from a run's process, before
anything is read, and it is never covered by --yes: there is no non-interactive
form.

Usage: `fugaro creds set NAME`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--config` | string | "" | no | the project config file to use (default: the project's $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/fugaro/projects/<name>.yaml) |
| `--gcp-project` | string | "" | no | the GCP project ID; it must be the selected project config's gcp_project |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for set |
| `--json` | bool | `false` | no | print machine-readable output |
| `--project` | string | "" | no | the Fugaro project to act on (default: the checkout's fugaro.yaml project:, else $FUGARO_PROJECT, else the only project config) |
| `--region` | string | "" | no | GCP region (overrides the project config's) |

## `fugaro doctor`

Check that Fugaro is set up and ready, without changing anything

doctor only ever reads: the environment, Terraform, the local project config
and its installation's billing and IAM policy (with a budget backend, who can
sign sign-in tokens for it: warnings, never changes), the Fugaro plugin's wiring in
.claude/settings.json, a checkout's fugaro.yaml and its stored secrets by
name. With --check-github-app, in your own terminal, it also asks GitHub whether
each GitHub App the config records is installed on its repository with the
permissions Fugaro's runs ask for: that is the one thing that reads a secret's
value (the App's private key, with your own credentials, held in memory only to
sign, never printed), and it is refused in a coding agent's session. With
--check-bitbucket-token, in your own terminal, it also reads the credentials
service's bundle to see that it holds a Bitbucket token and asks Bitbucket
whether it still accepts it, one GET /repositories/<repo> per proxied
repository: that too reads a secret's value (with your own credentials, in
memory only, never printed) and is refused in a coding agent's session.
Otherwise it never prints a secret's value and never creates, enables or
changes anything.

Inside a checkout whose project publishes a project layer (fugaro config
publish), doctor also names which layer applies, flags a run that launched
without it or on an older generation, a stale per-repository copy (the one
Cloud Build and the daily image check read), and a workflow whose image was
last built from settings it no longer resolves to: every one of these
degrades with a note instead of failing when the bucket is unreachable.

--plugin checks only the plugin's wiring: offline, no credentials, safe for
CI. --strict makes a stale, unpinned, foreign or unwired plugin fail the
command; the informational states ("not installed", "cannot compare") never
do, with or without --strict. A repository's CI runs
fugaro doctor --plugin --strict.

With no local Fugaro installation configured, doctor says so and names
fugaro setup as the fix, rather than guessing at a project.

What doctor prints is a verdict and then only what to do: one sentence and one
fix per item, each item fugaro update puts right ending in that command.
--all prints every check, the informational lines included, and --security the
IAM and security sweep (who can read a stored credential, who can sign a
budget token, what a launcher may start). The default view never hides a
security finding that is a warning, and it says how many findings it left out
when it leaves any out. Every check, with its full text, is in --json whatever
the flags.

Exit 1 when a check fails, with the one-line fix to run.

Usage: `fugaro doctor [--json] [--all] [--security] [--plugin] [--strict]`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--all` | bool | `false` | no | print every check, the informational and audit lines included |
| `--check-bitbucket-token` | bool | `false` | no | also check the credentials service's bundle holds a Bitbucket token and that Bitbucket still accepts it: reads the bundle with your own credentials, in memory only, for one GET /repositories/<repo> per proxied repository (refused in a coding agent's session; GODEBUG=http2debug would print the token, so unset it) |
| `--check-github-app` | bool | `false` | no | also check each recorded GitHub App is installed with the permissions runs ask for: reads the App's private key from Secret Manager with your own credentials, in memory only, for one signed token (refused in a coding agent's session; GODEBUG=http2debug would print the token, so unset it) |
| `--config` | string | "" | no | the project config file to use (default: the project's $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/fugaro/projects/<name>.yaml) |
| `--dir` | string | `.` | no | a directory in the checkout, for the plugin wiring |
| `--gcp-project` | string | "" | no | the GCP project ID; it must be the selected project config's gcp_project |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for doctor |
| `--json` | bool | `false` | no | print machine-readable output |
| `--plugin` | bool | `false` | no | check only the plugin's wiring (offline, no credentials) |
| `--project` | string | "" | no | the Fugaro project to act on (default: the checkout's fugaro.yaml project:, else $FUGARO_PROJECT, else the only project config) |
| `--region` | string | "" | no | GCP region (overrides the project config's) |
| `--security` | bool | `false` | no | also print the IAM and security sweep (who may read a credential, who may sign a budget token, what a launcher may start) |
| `--strict` | bool | `false` | no | fail on a stale, unpinned, foreign or unwired plugin (CI mode) |

## `fugaro image build`

Build the derived image with Cloud Build; --local builds it with local Docker and smoke-tests it

Build the workflow's derived image.

Without --local, Cloud Build builds it from the repository's base branch
as the repository's build account (cloning with its bitbucket-token, or
a read-only token its GitHub App mints) and pushes it to the repository's
own registry, which fugaro update --repo creates. It pushes a candidate,
smoke-tests it without network, and only then points latest at it and
records what it was built from, unless a newer build is already
recorded. Run it from the repository's checkout: the checkout's
fugaro.yaml and origin say what to build.

A Cloud Build is billable, so it asks for the project's name typed at a real
terminal: --json, a pipe and a coding agent's session never confirm it (it
prints the one line to run in your own terminal window and exits 1).
--local builds with your own Docker and costs nothing in the cloud.

Usage: `fugaro image build`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |

## `fugaro image check`

Decide whether each workflow's image needs a rebuild (the daily check; locally it only prints the decision)

Evaluate the rebuild triggers of the repository's workflows against the head of
its base branch: a blobless clone, the build record in the runs bucket, and the
base image's digest.

Run from a checkout, it uses your own git access and ADC and only prints each
workflow's decision: it never submits a build (--dry-run is accepted, and is what
it always does). Start a rebuild with fugaro image build.

With --job, as the repository's daily check job runs it (it refuses to submit
unless CLOUD_RUN_JOB or CLOUD_RUN_EXECUTION is set, as Cloud Run sets them, and
in a coding agent's session; --dry-run is always allowed), it reads the job's
spec from FUGARO_CHECK_SPEC, submits a Cloud Build rebuild when a trigger fires
(not with --dry-run), writes builds/<slug>/<workflow>/check.json, and logs one
JSON line per workflow. It exits 2 when the check itself failed.

Usage: `fugaro image check`

| `--dry-run` | bool | `false` | no | never submit a build (locally the check never does anyway) |
| `--force` | bool | `false` | no | decide rebuild whatever the triggers say (with --job: a build is submitted) |

## `fugaro image refresh`

Move a repository onto this release's base image: pin it, point the daily image check job at it, rebuild what is stale

Run it in the checkout of an onboarded repository, in your own terminal window
(or with --yes, unattended: see below).

It prints the whole plan first, then, each step with its own confirmation:
(2) resolves this release's base image of each selected workflow's kind at
its -pinned tag, verifies its cosign signature, reads the digest back
through the installation's remote repository and pins base_images.<kind> to
it, as fugaro update --base does (nothing is copied);
(3) points the repository's daily image check job at it (its image and
FUGARO_CHECK_SPEC's base images) through the Cloud Run Admin API, with no
Terraform; (4) rebuilds each selected workflow whose build record says it
was built from another base, or that has no build record or one that
cannot be read (billable: the project's name typed for each, or --yes);
(5) names fugaro update --anchor when fugaro.yaml lacks gcp_project.

A base_images entry that is neither this release's pin nor a release image
an earlier fugaro copied (a development or hand-pushed image) stops it
before anything changes, with or
without --yes: remove the entry from the local config, then rerun. It never
writes fugaro.yaml, never onboards a repository and never runs Terraform. A
coding agent's session is refused, --yes included (there is still no --json
or --plan-only to get around that). A run that stops says which steps
finished and what to rerun, --yes included when it was given; a rerun skips
what is done. Exit codes: 0 done, 1 a refusal or a confirmation not given,
2 a cloud failure.

Unattended use: pass --yes to run it from CI or a script, with no terminal.
It confirms every step, the base pin, the check-job update and EACH
billable build, with no cap on how many builds run: read the printed plan's
build count first. --yes does not cover a coding agent's session (refused,
same as without it) or a custom, dev or hand-pushed base image (still
refused with the one-line fix); there is still no --json or --plan-only.

Usage: `fugaro image refresh`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--config` | string | "" | no | the project config file to use (default: the project's $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/fugaro/projects/<name>.yaml) |
| `--expect-digest` | stringArray | `[]` | no | cross-check the digest of a base image's release signature, KIND=sha256:<hex>, as for the converge (repeatable) |
| `--gcp-project` | string | "" | no | the GCP project ID; it must be the selected project config's gcp_project |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for refresh |
| `--image-source` | string | "" | no | the registry and owner the release base images come from, as for the converge (default ghcr.io/dimipaun) |
| `--project` | string | "" | no | the Fugaro project to act on (default: the checkout's fugaro.yaml project:, else $FUGARO_PROJECT, else the only project config) |
| `--region` | string | "" | no | GCP region (overrides the project config's) |
| `--repo` | string | "" | no | owner/name of the repository; it must be this checkout's origin (refresh reads fugaro.yaml from the checkout) |
| `--workflow` | stringArray | `[]` | no | a workflow to refresh (repeatable; default: every workflow in fugaro.yaml) |
| `--yes` | bool | `false` | no | confirm every step without asking (the base copy, the check-job update and each billable build, with no cap on how many run), and without a terminal: for CI or a script. The plan is still printed first. Never confirmed in a coding agent's session (CLAUDECODE and the like): nothing is applied there, --yes included. Without --yes nothing changes: a real terminal and the typed confirmations are still required, as always |

deterministic gate over the saved plan rather than by a prompt.

This is not fugaro project (the project's own configuration) and not fugaro
setup (which creates and re-installs an installation): a managed project's
agent-authored root is applied by fugaro managed apply.

Usage: `fugaro managed`

| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |

## `fugaro managed apply`

Apply the agent-authored Terraform root of a managed project, as the deployer account

Apply the agent-authored Terraform root ROOT of a managed project.

ROOT is a directory in this repository's checkout (the checkout whose
fugaro.yaml names the project). Its files are copied into this command's own
workdir — never run in place, so terraform's plan file, lock file and provider
directory are not written beside the configuration under review — the state
backend is set to the project's own managed state bucket, the root is planned
into a saved plan file, the plan is gated against the project's managed
allowlist and against the addresses the project's OWNER approved, and the saved
plan file is applied as the project's deployer service account.

An address this command may delete or replace is never one of this command's
arguments: an approval lives in the owner's object at
gs://<runs bucket>/fugaro/allow-delete.json, written with the operator's own
credentials by fugaro allow-delete. This command registers no flag for one, so
there is no way to pass one.

The refusal this command's apply does not carry is the coding agent's: in a
managed project a coding agent's session applies cloud changes with no human
prompt, and what replaces the prompt is the gate (a refused plan is not
applied), the marker (an unreadable one is not an apply), the owner's list (an
address the owner did not approve is refused) and the deployer account (which
holds no project-level IAM permission and cannot write the runs bucket). None
of the four is a boundary against a session that goes around this program.

The prompt comes back whenever the whole-project inventory does not clear the
project: before anything is planned, this command reads every resource of the
GCP project (Cloud Asset, with the operator's own credential) and compares it
with what the installation's Terraform states account for. A resource nothing
accounts for, or an inventory that cannot be read, keeps this run's
confirmation: a coding agent's session is refused and a person is asked, with
the reason printed first. Nothing is halted and nothing is deleted.

Usage: `fugaro managed apply ROOT`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--config` | string | "" | no | the project config file to use (default: the project's $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/fugaro/projects/<name>.yaml) |
| `--gcp-project` | string | "" | no | the GCP project ID; it must be the selected project config's gcp_project |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for apply |
| `--project` | string | "" | no | the Fugaro project to act on (default: the checkout's fugaro.yaml project:, else $FUGARO_PROJECT, else the only project config) |
| `--region` | string | "" | no | GCP region (overrides the project config's) |

## `fugaro managed flag`

Flag an existing GCP project as managed (the project's owner)

Flag an existing GCP project PROJECT_ID as managed, recording the managed
marker in that project's own runs bucket.

This is how a project Fugaro did not create becomes managed: the marker is
what tells a later run that this project's applies may skip the typed
confirmation, and it is normally written by the run that created the project
(fugaro setup --create-project --managed). Flagging is the after-the-fact way,
answered by the owner on 2026-10-16 (design D58).

Run it in your own terminal, as an operator, with your own credentials, and
type the GCP project ID it asks for. A coding agent's session is refused, and
nothing stands in for the typed ID — not --yes, not --non-interactive, not a
pipe.

PROJECT_ID must be the exact GCP project ID of the installation selected by
--project, --config or the checkout: one invocation names one project, and
there is no bulk form, no wildcard and no prefix.

It records two things in gs://<runs bucket>/fugaro/managed.json: that this
project is managed, and the monthly budget amount and currency the owner
states with --budget and --budget-currency. The amount is required, with no
default (D64), because the marker's amount is what the apply-time budget read
opens the gate on: a marked project that records no amount is refused by every
managed apply rather than applied without a budget control. The amount is the
budget ALERT amount the installation's Terraform creates and nothing else —
this command does not create or change a budget, and it makes no billing call.

It writes BOTH marks a managed project carries, in one step: that object and
the label fugaro_managed=true on the GCP project itself (Task 3.0). The read
requires both — the label is what a project can be narrowed by, and a project
without it is not managed whatever its runs bucket holds — so writing the
object alone would leave this project exactly as unmanaged as it was. The
label is written on the project, by the account running this command, which is
why the account needs resourcemanager.projects.update on it; the project's
other labels are kept. A project that already carries that key with another
value is refused rather than overwritten — the label someone else put there is
a statement, not an empty slot — and the object written first is not taken
back, so that refusal says which half is there and which is missing.

What flagging gives up, stated before it writes: the marker is what turns the
typed confirmation off (D55), so from this project's next apply on, the
deterministic gate, the whole-project inventory, the owner-written delete list
(fugaro allow-delete) and the recorded budget are what stand in the
confirmation's place — and a coding agent's session can apply a plan the gate
admitted with no human prompt.

What it does not do: it is not a boundary against a session that goes around
this program. A coding agent's session holds the operator's credentials, can
write this object directly with gcloud storage cp, and can unset its own
marker and run this command; SECURITY.md records the wider Owner/Editor
bypass. The refusal below is a speed bump against an agent that uses the
program, not a wall against one that goes around it.

A project that already records an amount is refused: the amount is the owner's
decision at the time it was taken, and this command adds a budget rather than
editing one. The one object it does replace is a version-1 creation fact —
what fugaro setup --create-project without --managed leaves, and the state the
managed apply refuses for having no amount recorded. What it replaced is said
in the output, and the write is conditioned on the object it read, so nothing
is overwritten blind.

Usage: `fugaro managed flag PROJECT_ID`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--budget` | int64 | `0` | no | the monthly budget alert amount to record, in whole units of --budget-currency (required) |
| `--budget-currency` | string | "" | no | the currency --budget is in, three uppercase letters such as USD (required) |
| `--config` | string | "" | no | the project config file to use (default: the project's $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/fugaro/projects/<name>.yaml) |
| `--gcp-project` | string | "" | no | the GCP project ID; it must be the selected project config's gcp_project |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for flag |
| `--project` | string | "" | no | the Fugaro project to act on (default: the checkout's fugaro.yaml project:, else $FUGARO_PROJECT, else the only project config) |
| `--region` | string | "" | no | GCP region (overrides the project config's) |

## `fugaro pair`

Pair a phone with this installation

Pair a phone with this installation: the operator shows a QR code, the
phone scans it, writes its public key and shows a code derived from that
key, and the operator types the code back to bind the two.

Pairing is an admin act, and it needs both of the installation's two role
sets: the signer account's fugaroTokenMinter role to mint the pairing
token and the device token, and roles/firebasedatabase.admin to write the
device node and the delivery node.

Pairing is discovery, not identity: scanning the code tells the phone which
project and database to connect to and grants it no access by itself.

The code carries no key. The final credentials — the device token, the
per-pairing MAC key and the configuration the app stores — go to the phone
encrypted to the key it generated, and the MAC key never leaves this
laptop's OS keychain in clear, is never printed, and is not in the code.

The typed code is the binding: nothing is written to the project before the
code the operator types matches the key the phone wrote, so a refused
pairing leaves the project exactly as it was.

The code is drawn in a terminal wide enough for it. The payload is over a
kilobyte, so its code is over a hundred columns wide, and a narrower
terminal gets the payload line instead of a drawing that would wrap and
stop being a QR code; --json carries that same payload for a console.

Its own state is the local config: the project, its database URL and
Identity Toolkit API key, and the signer account. --json streams the
pairing as one JSON object per line on stdout for a console to read.

Usage: `fugaro pair`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--config` | string | "" | no | the project config file to use (default: the project's $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/fugaro/projects/<name>.yaml) |
| `--email` | string | "" | no | the administered email for the device (default, and normally the value: your own verified address, which is the only address this command may administer) |
| `--gcp-project` | string | "" | no | the GCP project ID; it must be the selected project config's gcp_project |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for pair |
| `--json` | bool | `false` | no | stream the pairing as newline-delimited JSON events on stdout |
| `--name` | string | "" | no | the device's name, for pair ls and the device node's own field |
| `--project` | string | "" | no | the Fugaro project to act on (default: the checkout's fugaro.yaml project:, else $FUGARO_PROJECT, else the only project config) |
| `--region` | string | "" | no | GCP region (overrides the project config's) |
| `--role` | string | "" | no | the device's role: viewer, operator or admin (default: your own role, inherited; --role may only lower it) |
| `--timeout` | duration | `2m0s` | no | how long to wait for the phone's key and the typed code (refused above 4m30s) |

Subcommands:

- `fugaro pair ls` -- List the devices paired with this installation
- `fugaro pair revoke` -- Revoke a paired device

## `fugaro pair ls`

List the devices paired with this installation

List the devices paired with this installation: one row per device node
under config/admin/devices, with the uid (a key, and therefore printable),
the name, the administered email, the role and the pairing time.

It reads with roles/firebasedatabase.admin, and it prints no token, no key
and no keychain item's value: the node holds none of them, and the item's
name is not in the node either, so there is nothing else to print.

It does not report whether a device's Auth user still exists. The Auth user
is not in the database, so database admin does not reach it, and the node's
existence is the whole of what the rules read (D166): an orphaned Auth user
whose node is gone is the history sweep's business and is invisible to the
rules by construction.

Its own state is the local config, as it is for the rest of the command.

Usage: `fugaro pair ls`

| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--config` | string | "" | no | the project config file to use (default: the project's $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/fugaro/projects/<name>.yaml) |
| `--gcp-project` | string | "" | no | the GCP project ID; it must be the selected project config's gcp_project |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for ls |

## `fugaro pair revoke`

Revoke a paired device

Revoke a paired device: the phone is off this installation's allowlist from
its next request on.

The order is the command (M4): the device node under config/admin/devices
goes first, because the node's existence is what the rules read and its
deletion revokes at once, without waiting for an ID token to expire; then
this laptop's OS keychain item for that pairing's MAC key. Two deletions,
and both are here.

The pairing session's own node is not one of them. Its key is the p~ uid
the session drew, and nothing on this laptop records that uid, so a revoke
by device cannot name the node it would delete; the history sweep deletes
it with the p~ user the node belongs to (mobile plan decision 2), and it
is the sweep this command names rather than a node it did not touch.

It does not delete the device's Auth user. No role a Terraform grant gives
an operator can delete one (the history job's account is the only holder of
roles/firebaseauth.admin), and the device node's deletion is what makes the
orphan the history sweep's to remove — which is why this command names the
sweep rather than pretending the account is gone.

Exactly one of --uid and --name selects the device, and a --name that
matches more than one node is refused rather than revoked ambiguously: the
refusal says how many it matched, and `fugaro pair ls` prints the uids to
pick one from.

Its own state is the local config, as it is for the rest of the command.

Usage: `fugaro pair revoke (--uid UID | --name NAME)`

Flags:

| Flag | Type | Default | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--config` | string | "" | no | the project config file to use (default: the project's $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/fugaro/projects/<name>.yaml) |
| `--gcp-project` | string | "" | no | the GCP project ID; it must be the selected project config's gcp_project |
| `-h`, `--help` | bool | `false` | no | help for revoke |
| `--json` | bool | `false` | no | print the revocation as one JSON event on stdout |
| `--name` | string | "" | no | the name of the device to revoke; it must match exactly one device |
| `--project` | string | "" | no | the Fugaro project to act on (default: the checkout's fugaro.yaml project:, else $FUGARO_PROJECT, else the only project config) |
| `--region` | string | "" | no | GCP region (overrides the project config's) |
| `--uid` | string | "" | no | the uid of the device to revoke (m~…), which is the node's key |

Subcommands:

This command has no subcommands.
